o: It is part of the panniculus carnosus
True. Platysma is part of the panniculus carnosus, lying in the superficial fascia, and is supplied by VII. (Last's)
It covers the external and anterior jugular veins
True. Platysma covers the external and anterior jugular veins and may help relieve pressure on them. (Last's)
It is supplied by the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve
By the cervical branch; proprioception via the transverse cervical nerve.
Its lateral border forms zygomaticus minor
It forms risorius, attached to the modiolus.

questions.s: The superficial part of the submandibular gland (Last's):
o: Its lateral surface is grooved by the facial artery
True. The facial artery grooves the back of the lateral surface of the gland as it hooks under the mandible. (Last's p. 436)
Its inferior surface is crossed by the facial vein
And the cervical branch of the facial nerve. (Last's p. 436)
Its medial surface lies mostly against hyoglossus
Mostly against mylohyoid; hyoglossus is overlapped posteriorly. (Last's p. 436)
It overlaps the masseter insertion
It overlaps the front of the medial pterygoid insertion. (Last's p. 436)

questions.s: The deep part of the gland and its duct (Last's):
o: The lingual nerve lies above the deep part
True. Between mylohyoid and hyoglossus the lingual nerve lies above the deep part, with the duct and XII below. (Last's p. 436)
The duct is about 5 cm long
The same length as the parotid duct. (Last's p. 436)
The hypoglossal nerve lies above the deep part
Below it, with the duct. (Last's p. 436)
The duct emerges from the deep part of the gland
From the superficial part near the posterior border of mylohyoid. (Last's p. 436)
Preganglionic fibres arise in the superior salivary nucleus
True. Secretomotor fibres start in the superior salivary nucleus, run in nervus intermedius and chorda tympani, and relay in the submandibular ganglion. (Last's p. 436)
Sympathetic fibres come from the plexus on the facial artery
True. Postganglionic sympathetic (vasoconstrictor) fibres reach the gland from the plexus on the facial artery. (Last's p. 436)
Preganglionic fibres run in the lesser petrosal nerve
Via nervus intermedius, chorda tympani and lingual nerve. (Last's p. 436)
All secretomotor cell bodies lie in the submandibular ganglion
A few lie in small ganglionic masses on the gland. (Last's p. 436)
It begins near the greater horn of the hyoid
True. The common carotid usually bifurcates at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, near the greater horn of the hyoid. (Last's p. 436)
It divides behind the neck of the mandible
Within the parotid. (Last's p. 436)
It lies lateral to the internal carotid at its origin
It is initially medial; the ICA is really lateral at its origin. (Last's p. 436)
The IJV lies medial to it at its commencement
Lateral at first, then posterior and deep. (Last's p. 436)

questions.s: Branches of the external carotid below the parotid:
o: There are six
True. Before entering the parotid the ECA gives six branches: three in front, two behind and one medial. (Last's p. 436)
The ascending pharyngeal is the medial branch
True. The ascending pharyngeal is the only medial branch, running up the pharyngeal wall beside the ICA. (Last's p. 436)
The occipital artery arises from the front
From behind, with the posterior auricular. (Last's p. 436)
The facial artery runs along the upper border of the posterior belly of digastric
The occipital and posterior auricular run along digastric's borders. (Last's p. 436)

questions.s: Separating the external from the internal carotid artery are:
o: The styloid process
True. The styloid process lies between the ECA (superficial) and ICA (deep). (Last's p. 436)
Stylopharyngeus
True. Stylopharyngeus passes between the two carotids from the styloid to the pharynx. (Last's p. 436)
The glossopharyngeal nerve
True. IX accompanies stylopharyngeus between the two arteries; so does the pharyngeal branch of X. (Last's p. 436)
The hypoglossal nerve
It crosses both carotids superficially. (Last's p. 436)
The internal vertebral plexus receives mainly basivertebral veins
True. Large basivertebral veins draining red marrow are the main tributaries of the internal vertebral plexus. (Last's p. 574)
It is a bypass of the diaphragm during raised abdominal pressure
True. When abdominal pressure rises, blood bypasses the IVC up the valveless plexus to the SVC, which also allows spread of cancer. (Last's p. 574)
The internal vertebral plexus has valves
There are no valves. (Last's p. 574)
The spinal dura fits tightly within the canal
Cord is narrower than dura, dura narrower than canal. (Last's p. 574)
It is the inner layer of posterior fossa dura continued
True. The spinal dura is the inner (meningeal) layer continued through the foramen magnum; the outer periosteal layer stops there. (Last's p. 574)
It attaches firmly to the PLL on the axis
And the tectorial membrane. (Last's p. 574)
It is firmly attached to the lumbar vertebral bodies
Elsewhere it is free of bony attachments. (Last's p. 574)
It ends at L2
At S2. (Last's p. 574)
The filum terminale perforates the theca at S2
True. The filum terminale pierces the dural sac at S2 and continues to the back of the coccyx. (Last's p. 574-5)
The lowest denticulation lies at the L1 root
True. The denticulate ligament's lowest tooth is at the level of the L1 root. (Last's p. 574-5)
The filum terminale ends at the tip of the sacrum
It descends to the back of the coccyx. (Last's p. 574-5)
The arachnoid strands are well developed in the anterior midline
In the posterior midline. (Last's p. 574-5)
The spinal subarachnoid space holds about 75 ml of CSF
True. About half the CSF (about 75 ml) is in the spinal subarachnoid space. (Last's p. 575)
The needle passes supraspinous then interspinous ligaments
True. A lumbar puncture needle passes skin, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, then dura and arachnoid. (Last's p. 575)
The spinal cord ends at L3 in the adult
At L1. (Last's p. 575)
Epidural anaesthetic is injected into the subarachnoid space
Into the extradural space. (Last's p. 575)
The carotid sinus wall contains baroreceptors
Supplied by the glossopharyngeal. (Last's p. 438)
The carotid body lies behind the bifurcation
True. The carotid body is a small structure behind the carotid bifurcation, supplied by glomic arteries. (Last's p. 438)
The carotid body is supplied by the ascending pharyngeal artery
By glomic arteries from the bifurcation. (Last's p. 438)
The carotid body is mainly innervated by the vagus
By the glossopharyngeal nerve. (Last's p. 438)

questions.s: Relations of the cervical internal carotid (Last's):
o: The sympathetic trunk lies behind it outside the sheath
True. The sympathetic trunk lies behind the ICA outside the carotid sheath, on the prevertebral fascia. (Last's p. 438)
The superior laryngeal nerve crosses obliquely behind it
True. The superior laryngeal nerve crosses obliquely behind the ICA to its medial side and divides there. (Last's p. 438)
It gives several branches in the neck
It has no branches in the neck. (Last's p. 438)
Its surface marking runs to the tragus
To the head of the mandible; the ECA line runs to the tragus. (Last's p. 438)
It leaves the posterior compartment of the jugular foramen
True. The IJV begins as the jugular bulb in the posterior, largest compartment of the jugular foramen. (Last's p. 438)
Its first tributary is the inferior petrosal sinus
True. The inferior petrosal sinus joins the IJV just below the skull base, as its first tributary. (Last's p. 438)
The thoracic duct crosses behind the right vein at C7
Behind the left vein. (Last's p. 438)
The inferior root of the ansa curls round its medial border
Its lateral border. (Last's p. 438)

questions.s: Tributaries and surface marking of the IJV:
o: The pharyngeal plexus joins above the facial vein
Last's order. (Last's p. 439)
The middle thyroid is the lowest named tributary
True. Below the inferior petrosal sinus the order is pharyngeal, facial, lingual, superior thyroid, then middle thyroid. (Last's p. 439)
The surface marking runs from the tragus to the sternal end of the clavicle
From the ear lobule. (Last's p. 439)
At 45 degrees the jugular pulse is normally seen at the angle of the mandible
Just above the clavicle. (Last's p. 439)
The vagus always lies between the IJV and ICA
True. The vagus lies deep in the sheath in the gutter between the IJV and the carotid arteries. (Last's p. 462)
The cervical sympathetic trunk lies behind it on the prevertebral fascia
True. The cervical sympathetic trunk lies behind the sheath on the prevertebral fascia, not in the sheath. (Last's p. 462)
The glossopharyngeal nerve curves backwards superficial to the IJV
The accessory does; IX curves forwards between ICA and ECA. (Last's p. 462)
The parotid lies medial to the sheath
The pharynx is medial; parotid lateral. (Last's p. 462)
Its medial boundary is the lateral pterygoid plate
True. The lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate forms the medial wall of the infratemporal fossa. (Last's p. 457)
Its lateral boundary is the ramus of the mandible
True. The ramus and coronoid process of the mandible form the lateral wall. (Last's p. 457)
Its posterior boundary is the posterior surface of the maxilla
That is anterior; the carotid sheath is posterior. (Last's p. 457)
Its roof is formed by the lesser wing of the sphenoid
By the infratemporal surfaces of greater wing and squamous temporal. (Last's p. 457)
Lateral pterygoid inserts into the pterygoid fovea
True. Both heads of lateral pterygoid insert into the pterygoid fovea on the neck of the mandible and into the disc. (Last's p. 458)
The superficial head of medial pterygoid arises from the maxillary tuberosity
And palatine pyramidal process. (Last's p. 458)
Lateral pterygoid closes the mouth
It opens the mouth, drawing condyle and disc forwards. (Last's p. 458)
Medial pterygoid is supplied by the anterior division of the mandibular nerve
From the main trunk. (Last's p. 458)
It passes between the neck of the mandible and sphenomandibular ligament
True. The maxillary artery enters the fossa between the neck of the mandible and the sphenomandibular ligament. (Last's p. 459)
Branches of its first and third parts enter bony foramina
Second part branches do not. (Last's p. 459)
The anterior tympanic artery enters through the squamotympanic fissure
Through the petrotympanic fissure; the deep auricular enters the squamotympanic. (Last's p. 459)
It usually passes above both heads of lateral pterygoid
Usually between the heads or deep to the lower head; rarely above. (Last's p. 459)

questions.s: Branches of the third part of the maxillary artery (Last's):
o: The pharyngeal artery enters the palatovaginal canal
True. The pharyngeal branch of the third part runs back through the palatovaginal canal with the pharyngeal nerve. (Last's p. 459)
The infraorbital artery passes through the inferior orbital fissure
True. The infraorbital artery enters the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure and runs forwards with the infraorbital nerve. (Last's p. 459)
It terminates as the greater palatine artery
As the sphenopalatine artery. (Last's p. 459)
The posterior superior alveolar artery arises from the second part
From the third part. (Last's p. 459)
It lies around and within lateral pterygoid
True. The pterygoid plexus surrounds and lies within lateral pterygoid. (Last's p. 460)
It acts as a peripheral heart for venous return
True. Contraction of the pterygoid muscles pumps blood through the plexus, acting as a "peripheral heart". (Last's p. 460)
It drains into the facial vein directly
Into the maxillary veins, forming the retromandibular vein with the superficial temporal. (Last's p. 460)
It has no connection with the inferior ophthalmic vein
It receives it via the inferior orbital fissure. (Last's p. 460)
It develops from the perichondrium of Meckel's cartilage
True. The sphenomandibular ligament is the perichondrium of Meckel's (first arch) cartilage. (Last's p. 460)
It is pierced by the mylohyoid nerve
True. The nerve to mylohyoid pierces it to reach the mylohyoid groove. (Last's p. 460)
The inferior alveolar nerve passes between it and the neck of the mandible
The auriculotemporal nerve and maxillary vessels do; inferior alveolar passes between it and the ramus. (Last's p. 460)
The mylohyoid groove is made by the mylohyoid nerve
By the mylohyoid vessels (vein). (Last's p. 460)

questions.s: The mandibular nerve in the infratemporal fossa (Last's):
o: It lies about 4 cm deep to the articular tubercle
True. The mandibular nerve lies about 4 cm deep to the articular tubercle, reached through the mandibular notch in a mandibular block. (Last's p. 460-2)
The otic ganglion lies on its deep surface
True. The small otic ganglion lies on the medial (deep) surface of the mandibular nerve. (Last's p. 460-2)
The auriculotemporal nerve lies below the maxillary artery
Above it. (Last's p. 460-2)
The lingual nerve enters the pharynx between middle and inferior constrictors
Between superior and middle constrictors. (Last's p. 460-2)
It lies between tensor palati and the mandibular nerve
True. The otic ganglion is sandwiched between tensor palati medially and the mandibular nerve laterally. (Last's p. 460-2)
It lies just below foramen ovale
True. It lies just below foramen ovale. (Last's p. 460-2)
It is round and about 1 cm across
2-3 mm, flat and applied to the nerve. (Last's p. 460-2)
Its parasympathetic root is the greater petrosal nerve
The lesser petrosal. (Last's p. 460-2)

questions.s: The glossopharyngeal nerve in the neck (Last's):
o: It curves forwards around the lateral side of stylopharyngeus
True. IX winds round the posterior then lateral side of stylopharyngeus, supplying it. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its pharyngeal branches join the plexus on the middle constrictor
True. Pharyngeal branches of IX join the plexus on the middle constrictor and are sensory. (Last's p. 462-5)
The tympanic branch leaves at the superior ganglion
At the inferior ganglion. (Last's p. 462-5)
It reaches the tongue in front of hyoglossus
Behind its posterior border. (Last's p. 462-5)
The external laryngeal nerve runs close to the superior thyroid vessels
True. The external laryngeal nerve runs close to the superior thyroid vessels, so it is at risk when they are ligated in thyroidectomy. (Last's p. 462-5)
The auricular branch supplies part of the outer tympanic membrane
True. The auricular branch of X supplies part of the external meatus and tympanic membrane (Arnold's nerve: the cough on cleaning the ear). (Last's p. 462-5)
The pharyngeal branch supplies stylopharyngeus
All pharyngeal muscles except stylopharyngeus. (Last's p. 462-5)
The right cervical cardiac branches pass in front of the subclavian artery
Behind it. (Last's p. 462-5)
It derives from the second arch
True. The styloid process and stylohyoid ligament come from second arch cartilage. (Last's p. 462-5)
The external carotid passes superficial to stylopharyngeus
Deep to digastric and stylohyoid. (Last's p. 462-5)
Stylopharyngeus arises low down in front
It is deepest and highest; styloglossus arises low in front. (Last's p. 462-5)
The three styloid muscles share one nerve supply
Each has a different supply. (Last's p. 462-5)

questions.s: The hypoglossal nerve in the neck (Last's):
o: It picks up a branch from C1
True. C1 fibres join XII and leave again in its "branches" (superior root of the ansa, thyrohyoid, geniohyoid, meningeal). (Last's p. 462-5)
It passes forwards just above the greater horn of the hyoid
True. XII runs forward just above the greater horn of the hyoid on hyoglossus. (Last's p. 462-5)
It lies superficial to the IJV
Deep to the veins. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its meningeal branch enters through the jugular foramen
Through the hypoglossal canal. (Last's p. 462-5)
The hard palate lies at C1
True. The hard palate is level with the anterior arch of the atlas (C1). (Last's p. 462-5)
The hyoid lies at C3
True. The hyoid lies at C3; the thyroid cartilage at C4-5 and the cricoid at C6. (Last's p. 462-5)
The cricoid lies at C4
At C6. (Last's p. 462-5)
The carotid pulse is felt against the C3 transverse process
Against the C6 (carotid) tubercle. (Last's p. 462-5)

questions.s: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia (Last's):
o: It splits to enclose sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
True. The investing layer splits to enclose sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, and the parotid and submandibular glands. (Last's p. 462-5)
It attaches to the hyoid
True. The investing layer is attached to the hyoid, which pulls sternocleidomastoid forward into a gentle curve. (Last's p. 462-5)
It forms the axillary sheath
The prevertebral fascia does. (Last's p. 462-5)
It attaches above to the inferior nuchal line
To the superior nuchal line. (Last's p. 462-5)
It extends down to T3
With longus colli. (Last's p. 462-5)
It is pierced by the four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus
True. The great auricular, lesser occipital, transverse cervical and supraclavicular nerves all pierce the prevertebral fascia. (Last's p. 462-5)
The accessory nerve lies deep to it
The accessory nerve lies superficial. (Last's p. 462-5)
The cervical sympathetic trunk lies deep to it
Superficial (in front). (Last's p. 462-5)
It is limited above by the strap muscle attachments
Hyoid and thyroid cartilage. (Last's p. 462-5)
It blends below with the fibrous pericardium
True. Below, the pretracheal fascia passes behind the brachiocephalic veins to blend with the arch adventitia and fibrous pericardium. (Last's p. 462-5)
The thyroid is attached to it at the first tracheal ring
The isthmus attaches at rings 2-4. (Last's p. 462-5)
It lies superficial to the strap muscles
It lies beneath them. (Last's p. 462-5)
The retropharyngeal space continues into the posterior mediastinum
True. The space in front of the prevertebral fascia runs from the skull base behind the pharynx and oesophagus into the posterior mediastinum, a route for spread of infection. (Last's p. 462-5)
The prevertebral space extends from skull base to T3
True. The prevertebral space lies behind the prevertebral fascia, from the skull base to T3. (Last's p. 462-5)
The retropharyngeal space lies behind the prevertebral fascia
In front of it, behind buccopharyngeal fascia. (Last's p. 462-5)
The parapharyngeal space is bounded medially by the pterygoid muscles
Laterally. (Last's p. 462-5)
It receives ipsilateral cortical innervation
Unlike any other muscle. (Last's p. 462-5)
It is supplied by the occipital and superior thyroid arteries
True. Sternocleidomastoid is supplied by branches of the occipital and superior thyroid arteries. (Last's p. 462-5)
The accessory nerve emerges at the junction of its lower and middle thirds
Halfway down its posterior border. (Last's p. 462-5)
It inserts into the lateral third of the clavicle
The medial third. (Last's p. 462-5)
The cervical plexus does not actually lie in the triangle
It is covered by SCM. (Last's p. 462-5)
The accessory nerve runs over levator scapulae in the roof fascia
True. Emerging from SCM halfway down its posterior border, XI crosses the triangle on levator scapulae within the roof fascia, very superficial and easily injured. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its roof is prevertebral fascia
The investing layer; prevertebral fascia forms the floor. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its base is the medial third of the clavicle
The middle third. (Last's p. 462-5)
The lesser occipital nerve is C2
True. The lesser occipital nerve (anterior ramus of C2) hooks round XI and runs up the back of SCM to the scalp behind the ear. (Last's p. 462-5)
The supraclavicular nerves are C3, 4
Mainly C4. (Last's p. 462-5)
The great auricular nerve is C4
The lesser occipital nerve comes from a posterior ramus
From the anterior ramus of C2. (Last's p. 462-5)
The great auricular nerve may thicken in tuberculoid leprosy
True. The great auricular nerve crosses SCM superficially and may become palpably thickened in tuberculoid leprosy. (Last's p. 462-5)
The lateral supraclavicular nerves reach halfway down deltoid
True. The lateral supraclavicular nerves cross the acromion to supply skin halfway down deltoid and back to the scapular spine. (Last's p. 462-5)
The transverse cervical nerve closely accompanies the transverse cervical artery
It is some distance from it. (Last's p. 462-5)
The third occipital nerve is an anterior ramus branch
Posterior ramus of C3. (Last's p. 462-5)
It is a branch of the nerve to subclavius
True. An accessory phrenic contribution (C5, 6) may run with the nerve to subclavius in front of the subclavian vein. (Last's p. 462-5)
It joins the phrenic in the superior mediastinum
True. It joins the main phrenic nerve in the superior mediastinum (or root of the neck). (Last's p. 462-5)
It arises from C3
From C5, 6. (Last's p. 462-5)
It passes behind the subclavian vein
In front of it. (Last's p. 462-5)
Stylohyoid embraces the digastric tendon
True. Stylohyoid splits round the intermediate tendon of digastric before inserting into the hyoid. (Last's p. 462-5)
Geniohyoid is supplied by C1 via the hypoglossal
True. Geniohyoid is supplied by C1 fibres that travel with XII. (Last's p. 462-5)
The anterior belly of digastric is supplied by the facial nerve
By the nerve to mylohyoid; the posterior belly by VII. (Last's p. 462-5)
Mylohyoid's anterior fibres insert into the hyoid
The posterior quarter inserts into the hyoid; the rest into the raphe. (Last's p. 462-5)
Sternothyroid is broader than sternohyoid and deep to it
True. Sternothyroid is the broader muscle, lying deep to sternohyoid and end to end with thyrohyoid. (Last's p. 462-5)
Omohyoid becomes tendinous over the IJV
True. Omohyoid's intermediate tendon lies over the IJV, a useful guide to the vein, and is slung to the clavicle by fascia. (Last's p. 462-5)
Thyrohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis
By C1 via the hypoglossal nerve. (Last's p. 462-5)
Sternothyroid inserts into the first costal cartilage only
Manubrium and first costal cartilage. (Last's p. 462-5)
The right arises behind the sternoclavicular joint
True. The right common carotid arises from the brachiocephalic trunk behind the right sternoclavicular joint; the left from the arch. (Last's p. 462-5)
It gives no branches below its bifurcation
True. The common carotid gives no branches until it divides into ICA and ECA. (Last's p. 462-5)
The sympathetic trunk lies within the sheath
Behind it, outside the sheath. (Last's p. 462-5)
The vagus lies medial to the common carotid
Between it and the IJV. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its inferior root spirals from behind the IJV
True. The inferior root (C2, 3) spirals round the lateral side of the IJV to join the superior root in front of the vein. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its superior root runs down in front of the IJV
True. The superior root (C1 via XII) descends in front of the IJV and carotids, embedded in the sheath. (Last's p. 462-5)
It lies within the posterior wall of the carotid sheath
The anterior wall. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its superior root is formed by C2
By C1 hitch-hiking with XII. (Last's p. 462-5)
Sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion travel with the superior thyroid artery
True. Vasoconstrictor fibres from the superior cervical ganglion reach the thyroid along the superior thyroid artery. (Last's p. 462-5)
Middle cervical ganglion fibres travel with the inferior thyroid artery
True. Fibres from the middle cervical ganglion travel along the inferior thyroid artery. (Last's p. 462-5)
Thyroid secretion is under vagal control
The vagal role is unknown; sympathetic fibres are vasoconstrictor. (Last's p. 462-5)
Mylohyoid separates the neck from the nasopharynx
It separates the mouth from the neck. (Last's p. 462-5)
The superior thyroid artery is its first anterior branch
True. The superior thyroid artery is the first (lowest) anterior branch, arising near the bifurcation. (Last's p. 437-8)
The external laryngeal nerve lies behind the superior thyroid artery
True. The external laryngeal nerve runs just behind the superior thyroid artery, so it is at risk when ligating at the upper pole. (Last's p. 437-8)
The lingual artery runs superficial to hyoglossus
Deep to it; the hypoglossal nerve is superficial. (Last's p. 437-8)
The facial artery gives the submental artery after crossing the mandible
Just before crossing it. (Last's p. 437-8)

questions.s: The occipital and posterior auricular arteries (Last's):
o: The posterior auricular gives the stylomastoid branch
Supplying the facial nerve and stapedial artery. (Last's p. 437-8)
The occipital artery runs with the greater occipital nerve
True. The occipital artery reaches the scalp with the greater occipital nerve, lateral to semispinalis capitis. (Last's p. 437-8)
The posterior auricular arises below digastric
Above digastric, sometimes in the parotid. (Last's p. 437-8)
The lower SCM branch of the occipital artery guides to the accessory nerve
The upper branch does; the lower holds the hypoglossal down. (Last's p. 437-8)

questions.s: Relations of the internal jugular vein (Last's):
o: The jugulo-omohyoid node lies behind it above omohyoid
True. The jugulo-omohyoid node lies behind the IJV just above omohyoid; it drains the tongue. (Last's p. 438)
The phrenic nerve lies behind it on scalenus anterior
True. The phrenic nerve on scalenus anterior and the cervical plexus lie behind the IJV. (Last's p. 438)
The transverse cervical artery lies in front of the IJV
Between scalenus anterior and the IJV. (Last's p. 438)
The facial vein is its first tributary
The inferior petrosal sinus is the first. (Last's p. 438)
The carotid triangle is bounded by SCM, posterior belly of digastric and superior belly of omohyoid
True. The carotid triangle is bounded by SCM, posterior belly of digastric and superior belly of omohyoid; it contains the carotid bifurcation. (Last's p. 438)
The submental triangle contains the anterior jugular vein
True. The submental triangle (between the anterior bellies of digastric and the hyoid) contains the anterior jugular vein and submental nodes. (Last's p. 438)
The posterior auricular artery arises within the carotid triangle
All ECA branches except the posterior auricular arise there. (Last's p. 438)
The digastric triangle is bounded below by the hyoid body
By the two bellies of digastric; the hyoid bounds the submental triangle. (Last's p. 438)
Rectus capitis lateralis runs from atlas to the jugular process
True. Rectus capitis lateralis runs from the atlas transverse process to the jugular process of the occipital bone. (Last's p. 440)
Longus capitis arises from C3-6 anterior tubercles
True. Longus capitis arises from the anterior tubercles of C3-6 and inserts into the basiocciput. (Last's p. 440)
Rectus capitis anterior runs from the axis to the foramen magnum
From the atlas lateral mass. (Last's p. 440)
Longus colli is supplied by posterior rami
By anterior rami. (Last's p. 440)

questions.s: The pyramidal space beside scalenus anterior (Last's):
o: Its apex is the carotid tubercle
True. The pyramidal space between longus colli and scalenus anterior has its apex at the carotid tubercle of C6. (Last's p. 440)
It contains the vertebral artery and stellate ganglion
And vertebral vein. (Last's p. 440)
It has a fascial roof
There is no fascial roof. (Last's p. 440)
Its base is the clavicle
The subclavian artery and neck of the first rib. (Last's p. 440)
The superior ganglion gives grey rami to C1-4
True. The superior cervical ganglion gives grey rami to C1-4, the middle to C5-6 and the inferior to C7-8. (Last's p. 440)
The middle ganglion lies near the C6 carotid tubercle
True. The small, inconstant middle ganglion lies medial to the C6 carotid tubercle. (Last's p. 440)
The inferior ganglion gives grey rami to C5-6
To C7-8; the middle to C5-6. (Last's p. 440)
The ansa subclavia passes behind the subclavian artery
In front of it. (Last's p. 440)
The left superior ganglion's cardiac branch goes to the superficial cardiac plexus
True. Of the cervical sympathetic cardiac branches, only the left superior goes to the superficial cardiac plexus; the rest go to the deep plexus. (Last's p. 440)
The inferior ganglion gives a vertebral plexus
True. The inferior ganglion sends a large branch along the vertebral artery (the vertebral plexus). (Last's p. 440)
Middle ganglion branches on the inferior thyroid artery are somatic
Visceral only. (Last's p. 440)
The sympathetic trunk lies in front of the carotid sheath
Behind it. (Last's p. 440)
It is supplied by C4, 5, 6
True. Scalenus anterior is supplied by the anterior rami of C4, 5 and 6. (Last's p. 444)
The subclavian vein lies in front of it
Free to dilate. (Last's p. 444)
The subclavian artery passes in front of it
Behind it (second part). (Last's p. 444)
The third part of the subclavian artery lies in front of the prevertebral fascia
Behind it. (Last's p. 444)
Scalenus medius arises from all cervical vertebrae
True. Scalenus medius arises from the posterior tubercles and lamellae of all the cervical vertebrae. (Last's p. 444)
Scalenus posterior inserts into the second rib
True. Scalenus posterior crosses the first rib to insert into the outer border of the second rib. (Last's p. 444)
Scalenus posterior inserts into the first rib
The second rib. (Last's p. 444)
The dorsal scapular artery passes in front of scalenus anterior
In front of scalenus medius, through the plexus. (Last's p. 444)
The suprapleural membrane forms its floor
True. The suprapleural membrane closes the thoracic inlet over the dome of the pleura. (Last's p. 444)
The recurrent laryngeal nerves run between trachea and oesophagus
True. In the root of the neck the recurrent laryngeal nerves run up in the groove between trachea and oesophagus. (Last's p. 444)
The costocervical trunk arises from the first part of the subclavian
From the second part. (Last's p. 444)
The internal thoracic artery arises from the upper surface of the subclavian
From its lower surface. (Last's p. 444)
They develop from second arch mesoderm
True. Facial muscles derive from second arch mesoderm and so are supplied by VII. (Last's p. 445-9)
The pterygomandibular raphe interdigitates with the superior constrictor
True. The pterygomandibular raphe joins buccinator in front to the superior constrictor behind. (Last's p. 445-9)
The marginal mandibular branch lies below the angle in about 50%
In about 20%. (Last's p. 445-9)
Buccal branch paralysis prevents blinking
It prevents emptying of the cheek pouch; zygomatic branch loss prevents blinking. (Last's p. 445-9)
Skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve
True. The great auricular nerve (C2, 3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, the only facial skin not supplied by V. (Last's p. 450-1)
The lower eyelid is supplied by V2
True. The lower lid is supplied by palpebral branches of the infraorbital nerve (V2). (Last's p. 450-1)
The ophthalmic division has three cutaneous branches
Five; maxillary and mandibular three each. (Last's p. 450-1)
The infratrochlear nerve supplies the lower eyelid
Medial upper lid and bridge of nose. (Last's p. 450-1)
The angular vein becomes the facial vein below the mandible
True. The supraorbital and supratrochlear veins form the angular vein, which becomes the facial vein. (Last's p. 450-1)
The posterior branch of the retromandibular vein joins the posterior auricular to form the EJV
True. The posterior division of the retromandibular vein joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein. (Last's p. 450-1)
The superficial temporal vein joins the facial vein to form the retromandibular vein
It joins the maxillary vein. (Last's p. 450-1)
The deep facial vein connects the facial vein to the cavernous sinus directly
To the pterygoid plexus. (Last's p. 450-1)
Its neurovascular plane is the dense connective tissue layer
True. Vessels and nerves run in the dense connective tissue (second layer), where vessels are held open, so scalp wounds bleed freely. (Last's p. 452-4)
Scalp skin is the thickest in the body
True. Scalp skin is the thickest skin in the body. (Last's p. 452-4)
The two occipitalis muscles join in the midline
The frontal bellies meet; the occipital bellies do not. (Last's p. 452-4)
Frontalis has a bony origin
Only occipitalis does. (Last's p. 452-4)

questions.s: Nerves and vessels of the scalp (Last's):
o: The middle temporal vessels pierce temporalis fascia
True. The middle temporal vessels pierce the temporalis fascia to reach the muscle. (Last's p. 452-4)
Frontalis is supplied by temporal and zygomatic branches of VII
True. Frontalis is supplied by temporal and upper zygomatic branches of VII; occipitalis by the posterior auricular branch. (Last's p. 452-4)
The greater occipital nerve is an anterior ramus
Posterior ramus of C2. (Last's p. 452-4)
The superficial temporal vessels pierce temporalis fascia
They lie on it. (Last's p. 452-4)
Its posterior fibres retract the mandible
The only retractor. (Last's p. 454-5)
It is supplied by deep temporal nerves
True. Temporalis is supplied by two or three deep temporal branches of the anterior division of V3. (Last's p. 454-5)
Its anterior fibres are horizontal
Vertical; posterior fibres horizontal. (Last's p. 454-5)
It inserts into the condylar process
Into the coronoid process and front of the ramus. (Last's p. 454-5)
It has three heads fused anteriorly
True. The superficial, intermediate and deep heads are fused anteriorly and diverge behind. (Last's p. 454-5)
The masseteric nerve runs between deep and intermediate parts
True. The masseteric nerve runs between the deep and intermediate parts; the masseteric artery between the intermediate and superficial parts. (Last's p. 454-5)
It retracts the mandible
It elevates and protracts. (Last's p. 454-5)
Its superficial part arises from the posterior third of the arch
From the anterior two-thirds of the lower border. (Last's p. 454-5)
From superficial to deep: facial nerve, retromandibular vein, ECA
True. From superficial to deep in the parotid: facial nerve, retromandibular vein, external carotid artery. (Last's p. 455-7)
Its upper pole adheres to the cartilage of the external meatus
True. The small upper pole is moulded against the cartilaginous meatus near the TMJ capsule. (Last's p. 455-7)
The ECA is its most superficial content
The facial nerve is most superficial. (Last's p. 455-7)
The parotid fascia is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve
By the great auricular; the gland by the auriculotemporal. (Last's p. 455-7)
Secretomotor fibres relay in the otic ganglion
True. Inferior salivary nucleus → IX → tympanic branch → lesser petrosal → relay in the otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve to the gland. (Last's p. 455-7)
Sympathetic fibres travel with the middle meningeal artery
True. Sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion reach the gland via the plexus on the external carotid and middle meningeal artery. (Last's p. 455-7)
Secretomotor fibres arise in the superior salivary nucleus
Inferior salivary nucleus. (Last's p. 455-7)
Postganglionic fibres travel in the facial nerve
In the auriculotemporal nerve. (Last's p. 455-7)
The ganglion lies in front of the pterygoid canal
Below and medial to the maxillary nerve. (Last's p. 466-70)
It is called the ganglion of hay fever
True. The pterygopalatine ganglion is called the ganglion of hay fever because it is secretomotor to the nasal glands and lacrimal gland. (Last's p. 466-70)
The lesser palatine nerves supply the hard palate
The soft palate and tonsil. (Last's p. 466-70)
The olfactory area extends below the superior concha
Over but not below it. (Last's p. 466-70)
The zygomatic nerve runs above the maxillary nerve in the fissure
True. The zygomatic nerve runs above the maxillary nerve in the inferior orbital fissure before turning up the lateral orbital wall. (Last's p. 466-70)
The middle meningeal nerve supplies the front half of the middle fossa
True. The middle meningeal branch of V2 supplies the dura of the anterior half of the middle fossa. (Last's p. 466-70)
The posterior superior alveolar nerve passes through the inferior orbital fissure
Through the pterygomaxillary fissure. (Last's p. 466-70)
The ganglionic branches are multiple slender twigs
A single stout trunk. (Last's p. 466-70)
The sphenoidal sinus opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess
True. The sphenoidal sinus opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha. (Last's p. 470-3)
The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus
True. The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus, guarded by a mucosal fold. (Last's p. 470-3)
Posterior ethmoidal cells open into the middle meatus
Into the superior meatus. (Last's p. 470-3)
The sphenopalatine foramen lies beneath the posterior end of the inferior concha
Beneath the middle concha. (Last's p. 470-3)

questions.s: Nerve supply of the nasal cavity (Last's):
o: The vestibule is supplied by the infraorbital nerve
True. Branches of the infraorbital nerve creep in from the face to supply the vestibule of the nose. (Last's p. 470-3)
The anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the lower front of the lateral wall
True. The anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the front of the lateral wall and floor of the nose. (Last's p. 470-3)
The nasopalatine nerve supplies the lateral wall
It supplies the septum. (Last's p. 470-3)
The olfactory area extends onto the inferior concha
Roof, septum and superior concha only. (Last's p. 470-3)
Its floor lies lower than the floor of the nose
True. The alveolar floor of the maxillary sinus usually lies lower than the floor of the nose, near the molar roots. (Last's p. 474-6)
Its ostium opens at the posterior end of the semilunar hiatus
True. The maxillary ostium opens high on the medial wall at the back of the semilunar hiatus, so it drains poorly when upright. (Last's p. 474-6)
Its apex points to the frontal process of the maxilla
To the zygomatic process. (Last's p. 474-6)
Its ostium lies low on the medial wall
High up, so drainage is poor. (Last's p. 474-6)

questions.s: The ethmoidal, sphenoidal and frontal sinuses (Last's):
o: Posterior ethmoidal cells receive both V1 and V2 fibres
Hence referred pain to both. (Last's p. 474-6)
The frontal sinus is supplied by the supraorbital nerve
And supratrochlear. (Last's p. 474-6)
The sphenoidal sinuses are usually symmetrical
Usually asymmetrical. (Last's p. 474-6)
The frontal sinus drains into the posterior end of the semilunar hiatus
Into its front end. (Last's p. 474-6)
The pituitary fossa lies above it
True. The pituitary fossa sits on the roof of the sphenoidal sinus, allowing the transsphenoidal approach. (Last's p. 474-6)
The internal carotid artery lies lateral to it
True. The cavernous sinus and ICA lie lateral to the sphenoidal sinus and may ridge its wall. (Last's p. 474-6)
The pons lies above it
Behind it, in the posterior fossa. (Last's p. 474-6)
The nerve of the pterygoid canal may ridge its roof
Its floor. (Last's p. 474-6)

questions.s: Nerve supply of the mouth, teeth and gums (Last's):
o: The greater palatine nerve supplies palate to the incisive foramen
True. The greater palatine nerve supplies the hard palate and palatal gum forward to the incisive foramen; the nasopalatine supplies in front of it. (Last's p. 477)
The lingual nerve supplies the lower lingual gums
True. The lingual nerve supplies the lingual gum of the lower teeth. (Last's p. 477)
The middle superior alveolar nerve supplies the canines
The anterior superior alveolar does. (Last's p. 477)
The buccal nerve supplies the red margin of the lower lip
The mental nerve does. (Last's p. 477)
The foramen caecum is the remnant of the thyroglossal duct
True. The foramen caecum at the apex of the sulcus terminalis marks where the thyroglossal duct began. (Last's p. 480-4)
The vallecula's anterior wall is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve
True. The anterior wall of the vallecula is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve (fourth arch). (Last's p. 480-4)
Palatoglossus is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve
By the pharyngeal plexus (vagus). (Last's p. 480-4)
The second arch contributes to the tongue mucosa
It is not represented, overgrown by the third. (Last's p. 480-4)
The lingual nerve lies on its superficial surface
With duct and hypoglossal nerve. (Last's p. 480-4)
The lingual artery lies deep to it
With the glossopharyngeal nerve and stylohyoid ligament. (Last's p. 480-4)
The hypoglossal nerve lies deep to it
Superficial. (Last's p. 480-4)
It arises from the lesser horn of the hyoid
From the greater horn. (Last's p. 480-4)

questions.s: The lingual nerve in the mouth (Last's):
o: It enters the mouth below the superior constrictor at the lower end of the raphe
True. The lingual nerve enters the mouth below the lower border of the superior constrictor, at the lower end of the pterygomandibular raphe. (Last's p. 480-4)
The submandibular ganglion hangs from it on hyoglossus
True. The submandibular ganglion hangs from the lingual nerve on the surface of hyoglossus. (Last's p. 480-4)
It lies against the mandible at the second premolar
At the posterior border of the third molar. (Last's p. 480-4)
Its gingival branch supplies the buccal gum
The lingual gum. (Last's p. 480-4)
It is about 12 cm long
True. The pharynx is about 12 cm long, from the skull base to C6. (Last's p. 486-9)
It becomes the oesophagus at C6
True. The pharynx becomes the oesophagus at the lower border of the cricoid (C6). (Last's p. 486-9)
The pharyngobasilar fascia attaches to the lateral pterygoid plate
To the medial plate. (Last's p. 486-9)
The cartilaginous auditory tube enters below the pharyngobasilar fascia
Above it. (Last's p. 486-9)
The middle constrictor arises from the stylohyoid ligament and greater horn
True. The middle constrictor arises from the angle between the stylohyoid ligament and the greater horn of the hyoid. (Last's p. 486-9)
The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane between middle and inferior constrictors
True. The gap between middle and inferior constrictors is closed by the thyrohyoid membrane, pierced by the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels. (Last's p. 486-9)
The glossopharyngeal nerve passes between middle and inferior constrictors
Between superior and middle. (Last's p. 486-9)
The recurrent laryngeal nerve passes deep to the upper border of the inferior constrictor
The lower border. (Last's p. 486-9)
Palatopharyngeus is the most internal muscle of the wall
True. Palatopharyngeus lies internal to all the other muscles of the pharyngeal wall. (Last's p. 486-9)
Stylopharyngeus is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve
True. Stylopharyngeus is the only muscle supplied by IX. (Last's p. 486-9)
Salpingopharyngeus arises from the hamulus
From the cartilage of the auditory tube. (Last's p. 486-9)
The pharyngeal plexus lies mainly over the superior constrictor
Over the middle constrictor. (Last's p. 486-9)
The nasopharynx is supplied by the pharyngeal branch of the pterygopalatine ganglion
Via the palatovaginal canal. (Last's p. 486-9)
The oropharynx is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve
True. The oropharynx is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (the afferent limb of the gag reflex). (Last's p. 486-9)
The tonsillar fossa floor is the middle constrictor
The superior constrictor. (Last's p. 486-9)
The gag reflex efferent is the glossopharyngeal
The afferent is IX; the efferent is X. (Last's p. 486-9)
It is supplied via the nerve to medial pterygoid
The only palatal muscle not supplied by the pharyngeal plexus. (Last's p. 492-5)
It turns around the hamulus
True. Tensor palati's tendon turns round the hamulus to spread out as the palatine aponeurosis. (Last's p. 492-5)
It arises from the petrous apex
Levator does; tensor arises from the scaphoid fossa, tube and sphenoid spine. (Last's p. 492-5)
It elevates the palate
It tenses it; levator elevates. (Last's p. 492-5)
It inserts into the nasal surface of the palatine aponeurosis
Between heads of palatopharyngeus. (Last's p. 492-5)
It forms a V-shaped sling
True. The two levators form a V-shaped sling that lifts the soft palate up and back. (Last's p. 492-5)
It is supplied by the mandibular nerve
By the pharyngeal plexus. (Last's p. 492-5)
It arises posterior to the carotid canal
Anterior to it on the petrous apex. (Last's p. 492-5)
The recurrent laryngeal nerve lies behind the cricothyroid joint
True. The recurrent laryngeal nerve passes under the inferior constrictor just behind the cricothyroid joint. (Last's p. 496-505)
The cricothyroid muscle derives from the 4th arch
True. Cricothyroid is a fourth arch muscle, supplied by the external laryngeal nerve. (Last's p. 496-505)
The superior laryngeal artery arises from the inferior thyroid artery
From the superior thyroid. (Last's p. 496-505)
The inferior laryngeal artery enters through the thyrohyoid membrane
With the recurrent nerve under the inferior constrictor. (Last's p. 496-505)
Laryngeal sensory cell bodies are in the inferior vagal ganglion
True. Sensory fibres from the larynx have cell bodies in the inferior vagal ganglion. (Last's p. 496-505)
The recurrent nerve often divides at the upper border of the thyroid isthmus
True. The recurrent nerve often divides into two at the level of the upper border of the thyroid isthmus. (Last's p. 496-505)
Cricothyroid is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve
By the external laryngeal. (Last's p. 496-505)
The internal laryngeal nerve supplies mucosa below the vocal folds
Above the folds. (Last's p. 496-505)
The medial walls of the two orbits are parallel
True. The medial orbital walls are parallel; the lateral walls diverge at about 90 degrees to each other. (Last's p. 505-6)
The marginal tubercle of Whitnall is on the zygomatic bone
True. Whitnall's marginal tubercle on the zygomatic bone gives attachment to the lateral palpebral ligament. (Last's p. 505-6)
The inferior orbital fissure lies between greater and lesser wings
The superior fissure does; the inferior lies between greater wing and maxilla. (Last's p. 505-6)
The ethmoidal foramina lie at the junction of medial wall and floor
Of medial wall and roof. (Last's p. 505-6)
Inferior oblique is the only ocular muscle not arising from the back of the orbit
True. Inferior oblique arises from the front of the orbital floor; all the others arise at the back. (Last's p. 508-11)
Lateral rectus has a C-shaped origin across the superior orbital fissure
True. Lateral rectus arises in a C-shape from the tendinous ring bridging the superior orbital fissure, so it is longer than the other recti. (Last's p. 508-11)
The superior oblique inserts in front of the equator
Behind the equator. (Last's p. 508-11)
The nerve to inferior oblique is the shortest nerve in the orbit
The longest muscular nerve. (Last's p. 508-11)
It arises from the under surface of the lesser wing
True. Levator palpebrae superioris arises from the under surface of the lesser wing at the apex of the orbit. (Last's p. 508-11)
Complete oculomotor palsy causes complete ptosis
True. A complete III palsy paralyses the striated levator, causing complete ptosis; sympathetic loss causes only partial ptosis. (Last's p. 508-11)
Its smooth muscle receives sympathetics from the middle cervical ganglion
From the superior cervical ganglion. (Last's p. 508-11)
The frontal nerve lies on its lower surface
Its upper surface. (Last's p. 508-11)
Seven nerves enter through the superior orbital fissure
True. III (two divisions), IV, VI and the lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves pass through the superior orbital fissure: seven in all. (Last's p. 511-12)
The frontal nerve gives no branches to orbital contents
Apart from periosteal twigs. (Last's p. 511-12)
The ciliary ganglion lies medial to the optic nerve
Lateral, a third of the way forward. (Last's p. 511-12)
The optic nerve meets the sclera 3 mm lateral to the posterior pole
3 mm medial. (Last's p. 511-12)

questions.s: The optic nerve in the orbit (Last's):
o: Its orbital length is about 3 cm
True. The optic nerve is about 3 cm long in the orbit, with slack to allow eye movement. (Last's p. 511-12)
The ophthalmic artery crosses it from lateral to medial
True. The ophthalmic artery spirals round the lateral side of the nerve and crosses above it from lateral to medial. (Last's p. 511-12)
The ophthalmic artery crosses it from medial to lateral
Lateral to medial. (Last's p. 511-12)
It lies outside the dural sheath in the orbit
Within dura and arachnoid to the back of the eye. (Last's p. 511-12)
Its secretomotor fibres relay in the pterygopalatine ganglion
True. Superior salivary nucleus → greater petrosal → nerve of pterygoid canal → relay in the pterygopalatine ganglion → zygomatic and lacrimal nerves. (Last's p. 511-12)
The lower eyelid is supplied by the infraorbital nerve
True. The lower eyelid and its conjunctiva are supplied by palpebral branches of the infraorbital nerve. (Last's p. 511-12)
Its secretomotor fibres arise in the inferior salivary nucleus
Superior salivary. (Last's p. 511-12)
The conjunctiva is supplied by a different nerve from the overlying lid
The same nerve. (Last's p. 511-12)
The lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves lie outside the cone of muscles
True. The lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves enter lateral to the tendinous ring and lie outside the muscle cone. (Last's p. 512-14)
The trochlear nerve enters the upper surface of superior oblique
Last's describes it sinking into the upper surface. (Last's p. 512-14)
The nasociliary nerve lies outside the cone
Inside, with III divisions and VI. (Last's p. 512-14)
The nerve to medial rectus passes above the optic nerve
Below it. (Last's p. 512-14)
Its parasympathetic root comes from the nerve to inferior oblique
True. Edinger-Westphal fibres reach the ciliary ganglion via the nerve to inferior oblique. (Last's p. 512-14)
It gives about 12 short ciliary nerves
True. About 12 short ciliary nerves leave the ganglion and pierce the sclera around the optic nerve. (Last's p. 512-14)
Most postganglionic fibres supply sphincter pupillae
Most supply the ciliary muscle; only about 3% supply the sphincter. (Last's p. 512-14)
Dividing its sensory root abolishes the conjunctival reflex
It abolishes the corneal reflex, not the conjunctival. (Last's p. 512-14)
The central retinal artery is its first and smallest branch
True. The central retinal artery is the first and smallest, but most important, branch: an end artery. (Last's p. 512-14)
The central artery enters the inferomedial part of the nerve halfway along
True. It enters the inferomedial side of the optic nerve about halfway between optic canal and eye. (Last's p. 512-14)
Central and posterior ciliary arteries anastomose freely
There is no anastomosis. (Last's p. 512-14)
It lies above the optic nerve in the optic canal
Below and lateral; the nerve joins it from above. (Last's p. 512-14)
The superior ophthalmic vein communicates with the angular vein
True. The superior ophthalmic vein begins above the medial palpebral ligament by joining the angular vein, linking face and cavernous sinus. (Last's p. 512-14)
The inferior ophthalmic vein drains partly to the pterygoid plexus
Through the inferior orbital fissure. (Last's p. 512-14)
The superior ophthalmic vein drains to the pterygoid plexus
Directly to the cavernous sinus. (Last's p. 512-14)
The inferior ophthalmic vein runs above the optic nerve
Within the cone below; the superior runs above the nerve. (Last's p. 512-14)
Superior rectus turns the eye up and in
True. Because of the angle between orbit and visual axes, superior rectus elevates and adducts (and intorts). (Last's p. 514-15)
Inferior oblique turns the eye up and out
True. Inferior oblique elevates and abducts (and extorts). (Last's p. 514-15)
Superior oblique causes extorsion
Intorsion, with superior rectus. (Last's p. 514-15)
Inferior rectus turns the eye down and out
Down and in. (Last's p. 514-15)
The pathway relays in the paramedian pontine reticular formation
Para-abducent nucleus. (Last's p. 514-15)
Crossed fibres ascend in the medial longitudinal bundle
To the contralateral oculomotor nucleus. (Last's p. 514-15)
The frontal eye field lies in the inferior frontal gyrus
In the middle frontal gyrus. (Last's p. 514-15)
Cold water caloric irrigation induces conjugate deviation to the opposite side
Ice water induces deviation to the same side. (Last's p. 514-15)
The sclera is an expansion of the optic nerve dural sheath
True. The sclera is continuous with the dural sheath of the optic nerve. (Last's p. 516-18)
The ciliary muscle is mesodermal
Sphincter and dilator are ectodermal. (Last's p. 516-18)
The cornea occupies the anterior third of the globe
The anterior sixth. (Last's p. 516-18)
Descemet's membrane is the anterior limiting layer
Bowman's is anterior; Descemet's posterior. (Last's p. 516-18)
The macula lies 3 mm lateral to the optic disc
True. The macula lies about 3 mm lateral to the optic disc at the posterior pole. (Last's p. 516-18)
The fovea contains only cones
True. The fovea has only cones, giving the sharpest vision. (Last's p. 516-18)
The optic disc is about 5 mm across
About 1.5 mm. (Last's p. 516-18)
The ganglion cells lie outermost, next to the pigment epithelium
They are innermost; light passes through them. (Last's p. 516-18)
The consensual reflex occurs because each pretectal nucleus reaches both Edinger-Westphal nuclei
And partial chiasmal crossing. (Last's p. 518-19)
Accommodation fibres bypass the pretectal nucleus
Explaining the Argyll Robertson pupil. (Last's p. 518-19)
Pupillary fibres run on the ventral surface of the oculomotor nerve near the brainstem
On the dorsal surface. (Last's p. 518-19)
Accommodation fibres pass through the posterior limb of the internal capsule
Through the anterior limb. (Last's p. 518-19)
It begins in the posterolateral hypothalamus
True. The ocular sympathetic pathway begins in the posterolateral hypothalamus and descends through the lateral brainstem. (Last's p. 518-19)
Preganglionic neurons are at T1
True. Preganglionic neurons are in the T1 lateral horn, leaving in the T1 white ramus. (Last's p. 518-19)
Postganglionic fibres reach the eye mainly via short ciliary nerves
Via the long ciliary nerves (nasociliary). (Last's p. 518-19)
Anhidrosis occurs with all Horner's lesions
Only central or preganglionic lesions. (Last's p. 518-19)
The external acoustic meatus is about 3 cm long
True. The external meatus is about 3 cm long: an outer cartilaginous third and an inner bony two-thirds. (Last's p. 523-6)
The deep auricular artery enters through the squamotympanic fissure
True. The deep auricular branch of the maxillary artery enters the meatus through the squamotympanic fissure. (Last's p. 523-6)
The extrinsic auricular muscles are supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve
By the facial nerve. (Last's p. 523-6)
The TMJ is supplied only by the auriculotemporal nerve
Also by the nerve to masseter. (Last's p. 523-6)

questions.s: Nerve supply of the external ear (Last's):
o: The great auricular supplies the cranial surface of the auricle
True. The great auricular nerve supplies the cranial surface and lower lateral surface of the auricle. (Last's p. 523-6)
The vagus supplies posterior meatal skin
True. The auricular branch of the vagus supplies the posterior meatal skin and part of the tympanic membrane. (Last's p. 523-6)
The auriculotemporal supplies the lower lateral auricle
The upper lateral surface and most meatal skin. (Last's p. 523-6)
The lesser occipital supplies most of the lateral surface
Only a small overlap at the top. (Last's p. 523-6)
The promontory is formed by the first turn of the cochlea
True. The promontory on the medial wall is the bulge of the basal turn of the cochlea. (Last's p. 526-8)
The pyramid lies on the posterior wall
Stapedius tendon emerges at its apex. (Last's p. 526-8)
The round window lies above and behind the promontory
Below and behind; the oval window lies above and behind. (Last's p. 526-8)
The trochleariform process lies on the lateral wall
On the medial wall. (Last's p. 526-8)
It is about 1 cm across
True. The tympanic membrane is about 1 cm across. (Last's p. 526-8)
It lies at about 55 degrees to the meatus
True. It lies obliquely at about 55 degrees, facing laterally, down and forwards. (Last's p. 526-8)
Its mucosal surface is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve
By the tympanic plexus (IX). (Last's p. 526-8)
The chorda tympani crosses lateral to the neck of the malleus
Medial to it. (Last's p. 526-8)
The stapes derives from the second arch
True. The stapes derives from second arch cartilage; the malleus and incus from the first. (Last's p. 528-9)
The anterior ligament of the malleus continues as the sphenomandibular ligament
True. The anterior ligament of the malleus passes through the squamotympanic fissure to the sphenoid spine as the sphenomandibular ligament (Meckel's remnant). (Last's p. 528-9)
The incus derives from the second arch
From the first arch, with the malleus. (Last's p. 528-9)
The anterior limb of the stapes is longer than the posterior
Shorter and straighter. (Last's p. 528-9)
Tensor tympani inserts into the handle of the malleus
True. Tensor tympani's tendon turns round the processus trochleariformis to insert into the upper handle of the malleus. (Last's p. 528-9)
Stapedius inserts into the neck of the stapes
True. Stapedius emerges from the pyramid and inserts into the neck of the stapes; it is supplied by VII. (Last's p. 528-9)
Tensor tympani relays in the otic ganglion
It passes near without relay. (Last's p. 528-9)
Stapedius lies in the upper semicanal of the musculotubular canal
Tensor tympani does; stapedius lies in the pyramid. (Last's p. 528-9)

questions.s: The tympanic plexus and lesser petrosal nerve (Last's):
o: The plexus is formed mainly by Jacobsen's nerve
Tympanic branch of IX. (Last's p. 529-31)
The lesser petrosal nerve emerges through a hiatus lateral to the greater petrosal
True. The lesser petrosal nerve emerges on the floor of the middle fossa through a small hiatus lateral to that of the greater petrosal. (Last's p. 529-31)
The lesser petrosal nerve leaves through the posterior wall
The anterior wall above the tube. (Last's p. 529-31)
Sympathetic fibres reach the plexus with the stylomastoid artery
Caroticotympanic nerves from the ICA. (Last's p. 529-31)
It is more than 3 cm long
True. The auditory tube is over 3 cm long: 1 cm bony and 2 cm cartilaginous. (Last's p. 529-31)
The isthmus lies posteromedial to the sphenoid spine
True. The narrowest part (isthmus), where bone meets cartilage, lies posteromedial to the sphenoid spine. (Last's p. 529-31)
Its bony part is longer than its cartilaginous part
The cartilaginous part (2 cm) is longer. (Last's p. 529-31)
Its cartilaginous part is supplied by the tympanic plexus
By the nervus spinosus; the bony part by the plexus. (Last's p. 529-31)
It is about 1 cm across
True. The mastoid antrum is about 1 cm across and adult-sized at birth. (Last's p. 529-31)
It connects to the epitympanic recess by the aditus
True. The aditus links the epitympanic recess to the antrum; the lateral canal and facial canal lie in its medial wall. (Last's p. 529-31)
It lies 5 mm deep to the suprameatal triangle
Mastoid air cells develop before birth
During the first year onwards. (Last's p. 529-31)
The cochlea makes 2.75 turns
True. The cochlea makes about two and three-quarter turns around the modiolus. (Last's p. 531-5)
The scala vestibuli and tympani communicate at the helicotrema
True. The scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate at the apex through the helicotrema. (Last's p. 531-5)
Endolymph and perilymph communicate freely
There is no communication. (Last's p. 531-5)
The perilymphatic duct opens into the internal acoustic meatus
Into the cochlear canaliculus at the jugular foramen. (Last's p. 531-5)
The anterior canal produces the arcuate eminence
True. The anterior (superior) canal lies across the long axis of the petrous bone and raises the arcuate eminence. (Last's p. 531-5)
There are five openings into the vestibule
True. Three canals open by five openings, because the anterior and posterior share a crus commune. (Last's p. 531-5)
The lateral canal opens by a crus commune
The anterior and posterior share the common crus. (Last's p. 531-5)
The posterior canal lies perpendicular to the long axis of the petrous bone
Parallel; the anterior is perpendicular. (Last's p. 531-5)
The stria vascularis produces endolymph
True. The stria vascularis on the outer wall of the cochlear duct produces endolymph. (Last's p. 531-5)
The saccule lies in the spherical recess
True. The saccule lies in the spherical recess, the utricle in the elliptical recess, of the vestibule. (Last's p. 531-5)
The utricle connects to the cochlear duct by the ductus reuniens
The saccule does. (Last's p. 531-5)
The maculae serve kinetic balance
Static; the cristae serve kinetic balance. (Last's p. 531-5)
The labyrinthine artery usually arises from AICA
Last's (it may also arise directly from the basilar). (Last's p. 531-5)
The labyrinthine vein drains to the inferior petrosal sinus
True. The labyrinthine vein drains to the inferior petrosal sinus. (Last's p. 531-5)
The vein of the vestibular aqueduct joins the inferior petrosal sinus
The superior petrosal sinus; the cochlear aqueduct vein joins the inferior. (Last's p. 531-5)
The stylomastoid artery does not supply the labyrinth
It assists. (Last's p. 531-5)
